ORDER:
The instant petition under Section 482 of Code of Criminal Procedure, 19731 has been filed by the Petitioners/Accused Nos.3 and 4, seeking to quash the proceedings against them in C.C.No.14 of 2012 on the file of Special Court under A.P.Protection of Depositors Financial Establishments Act-cum-VIII Additional District & Sessions Court(FTC), Vijayawada, which was registered for the offences punishable under Sections 420, 406 and 120-B read with 34 of the Indian Penal Code2 and Section 5 of the A.P.Protection of Depositors Financial Establishments Act3.

a. Accused No.1 is the Financial Institution, Accused No.2 is the Kartha of Hindu Undivided Family, Accused No.3 is the wife and Accused No.4 is the For short 'Cr.P.C' For short 'I.P.C.' For short 'the Act' brother of Accused No.2 and Accused No.5 is the brother-in-law of Accused Nos.2 and 4.
b.
Originally during the year 1974, father of Accused No.2 namely Kanduri Subrahmanyam established A.1 firm and collected deposits.

After his demise,
Accused No.2 during the year 1983, he took up the business of his father.
During the year 2004, Accused Nos.2 and 3 established A.1 firm consisting of Hindu Undivided Family of Accused Nos.2 and 3 and transferred the business to A.1 financial establishment.
c. While so, Accused Nos.2 to 5 conspired together dishonestly and fraudulently induced and allured the innocent public that they would return higher rate of interest Smt.

d. As such, based on reports of different depositors, cases in Crime Nos.131, 133, 143,
163183 and 184 of 2010 have been registered against Accused Nos.1 to 5 and as they are connected crimes and pertain to the same accused, after completion of investigation, a common charge sheet was filed in all the crimes and the same was numbered as C.C.No.14 of 2012.

Grounds Sought for Quashment 3. Aggrieved by the registration of the said case, Petitioners/Accused Nos.3 and 4 filed the present petition seeking quashment of the proceedings against them, on the following grounds;
a.
There is no allegation or overt act in the charge sheet to attract the offences under Sections 406 and 420 IPC.
b. Accused No.2 died on 16.02.2019.

Therefore, the charge sheet for the offences under Sections 406 and 420 IPC is liable to be quashed against Petitioners/Accused Nos.3 and 4 as there can be no inheritance of criminal liability of Accused Nos.1 and 2 on the Petitioners.
Therefore, continuation of criminal proceedings against the Petitioners/Accused Nos.3 and 4 is an abuse of process of law.

4. Heard T.Lakshmi Narayana, learned counsel for the Petitioners and Ms.D.Prasanna Lakshmi,
learned Assistant Public Prosecutor representing the State/Respondent.
5.
Learned counsel for the Petitioners would submit that the Petitioners have not committed any offence much less the alleged offence.
Criminal liability cannot be inherited on the Petitioners.
There are no specific overt acts attributed against the Petitioners.
Therefore, continuation of proceedings against the Petitioners is an abuse of process of law.
Hence, prayed to quash the proceedings against the Petitioners.

6. Per contra, learned Assistant Public Prosecutor would submit that, the Petitioners herein along with the other accused swindled and embezzled the public money for their personal use and thereby committed the offences as alleged against them.
There are specific allegations leveled against the Petitioners and prima facie case is made out against them.
Therefore, at this stage, Court cannot quash the proceedings against the Petitioners.
Accordingly, prays for dismissal of the petition.

7. Having heard the submissions of the learned counsel representing both the parties, now the point that would emerge for determination is:
Whether there are any justifiable grounds for quashment of proceedings against the Petitioners/Accused Nos.3 and 4 in C.C.No.14 of 2012 on the file of Special Court under A.P.Protection of Depositors Financial Establishments Act-cum- VIII Smt. Determination by the Court 8.

A bare perusal of Section 482 makes it clear that the Code envisages that inherent powers of the High Court are not limited or affected so as to make orders as may be necessary; (i) to give effect to any order under the Code or, (ii) to prevent abuse of the process of any Court or, otherwise (iii) to secure ends of justice.
A court while sitting in Section 482 jurisdiction is not functioning as a court of appeal or a court of revision.

It must exercise its powers to do real and substantial justice,
depending on the facts and circumstances of the case.
These powers must be invoked for compelling reasons of abuse of process of law or glaring injustice, which are against sound principles of criminal jurisprudence.
9. Specific circumstances warranting the invocation of the provision must be present.
The decision rendered by the Hon'ble Apex Court in State of Haryana and others v. Bhajanlal and others4 is considered as the guiding torch in the application of Section 482.

entities.text: State of Haryana and others v. Bhajanlal and others4
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
At paras 102 and 103, the circumstances are spelt out as follows;
4 AIR 1992 SC 604 "102.

In the backdrop of the interpretation of the various relevant provisions of the Code under Chapter XIV and of the principles of law enunciated by this Court in a series of decisions relating to the exercise of the extraordinary power under Article 226 or the inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code which we have extracted and reproduced above, we give the following categories of cases by way of illustration wherein such power could be exercised either to prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice, though it may not be possible to lay down any precise, clearly defined and sufficiently channelised and inflexible guidelines or rigid formulae and to give an exhaustive list of myriad kinds of cases wherein such power should be exercised.

(1) Where the allegations made in the first information report or the complaint, even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety do not prima facie constitute any offence or make out a case against the accused.

(2) Where the allegations in the first information report and other materials, if any,
accompanying the FIR do not disclose a cognizable offence, justifying an investigation by police officers under Section 156(1) of the Code except under an order of a Magistrate within the purview of Section 155(2) of the Code.

(3) Where the uncontroverted allegations made in the FIR or complaint and the evidence collected in support of the same do not disclose the commission of any offence and make out a case against the accused.

(4) Where, the allegations in the FIR do not constitute a cognizable offence but constitute only a non-cognizable offence, no investigation is permitted by a police officer without an order of a Smt. 4 Magistrate as contemplated under Section 155(2) of the Code.

entities.text: Smt. Kanduri Kanaka Durga, vs State Of Ap on 13 February, 2024 Indian Kanoon

sentences.text: (5) Where the allegations made in the FIR or complaint are so absurd and inherently improbable on the basis of which no prudent person can ever reach a just conclusion that there is sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused.

(6) Where there is an express legal bar engrafted in any of the provisions of the Code or the concerned Act (under which a criminal proceeding is instituted) to the institution and continuance of the proceedings and/or where there is a specific provision in the Code or the concerned Act, providing efficacious redress for the grievance of the aggrieved party.

(7) Where a criminal proceeding is manifestly attended with mala fide and/or where the proceeding is maliciously instituted with an ulterior motive for wreaking vengeance on the accused and with a view to spite him due to private and personal grudge.

103. We also give a note of caution to the effect that the power of quashing a criminal proceeding should be exercised very sparingly and with circumspection and that too in the rarest of rare cases;
that the court will not be justified in embarking upon an enquiry as to the reliability or genuineness or otherwise of the allegations made in the FIR or the complaint and that the extraordinary or inherent powers do not confer an arbitrary jurisdiction on the court to act according to its whim or caprice."
(emphasis supplied)
10.

In the case on hand, perusal of the material available on record would go to show that, Accused No.2 being Kartha of Hindu Undivided Family, took over the financial institution established by her father after his death.
Accused Nos.3 to 5 are the members of the Hindu Undivided Family.

It is alleged in the charge sheet that, by believing the inducement an allurement and on persuasion of Accused Nos.2 to 5, so many innocent public deposited huge amounts, during the period from 1994 to 2010 and Accused No.2 with a malicious intention with the active support of Accused Nos.3 to 5 executed promissory notes in the name of A.1-firm and in his personal capacity.

Further, Accused Nos.2 to 5 induced that they developed plots in different survey numbers at Paritala and Gottimukkala Villages and collected amounts from the public with a hope to get more interest and thereby all the accused dishonestly and fraudulently misappropriated the deposits collected from the public and used the said amounts for their personal use and to purchase properties.
To support the same, the Police filed the details of the depositors and the amounts invested by the in detail.

11. It is contended by the learned counsel for the Petitioners that since the offence under Sections 406 and 420 IPC has been committed by Accused No.2 and as he is no more, the criminal liability cannot be inherited to the Petitioners/Accused Nos.3 and 4.
Whereas the allegations of the charge sheet would disclose that Accused No.2 with the active support of Accused Nos.3 to 5, committed the alleged offences.
Therefore, it is not the stage to decide the veracity of the said allegations.

Truthfulness of the said contention can be revealed during the course of trial only.
The evaluation of the merits of the allegations made on either side cannot be resorted to at this stage and it is for the trial Court to evaluate the case on merits.
This case does not fall under any of the guidelines prescribed in Bhajanlal's case (supra).

12. Hence, this Court is of the view that the allegations made in the charge sheet, in this case, are sufficient enough for the trial to be taken up and thereby, the proceedings against the Petitioners/Accused Nos.3 and 4 are not advisable to be quashed and hence, the petition deserves dismissal.
13.
In the result, the Criminal Petition is dismissed.
Pending miscellaneous petitions, if any, shall stand closed.
